title: Innateness and Contemporary Theories of Cognition

summaries.example: Imagine a baby watching a toy disappear behind a screen. The baby looks longer when the screen seems to pass through the toy. Researchers think this may show that the baby expects the toy to keep existing even when it cannot be seen. The baby may begin with some built-in ideas about objects, although experience also helps develop richer knowledge.
summaries.summary: This entry explores a big question: are important parts of human thinking learned from experience, or are some present from birth? Empirists emphasize learning from what we see, hear, and do. Nativists say that people begin life with mental tools or expectations supplied by their biological nature. The debate became especially important after Noam Chomsky argued that children master complicated language even though they receive limited teaching and imperfect examples. This led researchers to ask whether children also begin with early knowledge in other areas. Studies of babies suggest that they may expect hidden objects to continue existing, compare approximate quantities, notice goal-directed actions, and respond to helpful or harmful behavior. These findings do not prove that every related idea is completely inborn. Children still need development, language, learning, and social experience. Other approaches, including connectionist and Bayesian theories, explain how experience can work together with starting abilities. The main lesson is that the simple question “Is this ability innate?” may have a mixed answer: different parts of thinking can have different beginnings.
key_ideas: Philosophers and scientists disagree about how much of the mind is built in and how much is learned.
Noam Chomsky helped revive interest in built-in abilities by studying how children learn complex language without much formal teaching.
Research suggests that young children may have early expectations about objects, approximate amounts, goals, and other minds.
Learning still matters. Even theories that support some built-in abilities usually allow experience and growth to develop them further.
summaries.why_it_matters: How our minds begin affects how we understand babies, learning, education, language, and human nature. If children have some early mental tools, teaching may build on them rather than start from nothing. If experience is more powerful than some researchers think, learning environments become especially important. The debate also shows how philosophy and experiments can work together: philosophical questions guide research, while research can challenge old ideas about what children understand.

important_terms.definition: The idea that some parts of our thinking are present from the beginning and do not have to be learned entirely from experience.
The view that knowledge is based mainly, or even entirely, on experience and learning.
A study method in which researchers watch how long a baby looks at an ordinary event and a surprising event.
The understanding that an object is still there even when it is hidden.

questions_to_think_about: When you learn a new game, which parts come from practice and which parts might come from abilities you already had?
Could a baby know something without being able to explain it with words?
Why might scientists use a baby’s looking time as evidence about what the baby expects?

summaries.example: Consider the classic false-belief problem. A child watches an adult place a toy in a box. The toy is moved while the adult cannot see. If the child expects the adult to search in the original box, the child appears to distinguish the adult’s belief from the toy’s actual location. Older studies treated success on this task as a key sign of a theory of mind, but studies of younger infants suggest that some understanding of goals and beliefs may appear earlier. This creates a further question: why can infants show some sensitivity in looking-time experiments while preschoolers may fail the standard verbal task?
summaries.summary:
The entry examines the contemporary revival of nativism, the view that some important cognitive resources belong to the organism’s initial condition. Its central contrast is with empiricism, which emphasizes experience and general learning. Historically, behaviorism treated psychology without reference to internal mental states and was associated with empiricist learning, although even behaviorist accounts presupposed innate behavioral repertoires. Chomsky’s work changed the debate by treating grammar as a psychologically real system of rules and by arguing that children acquire highly structured linguistic competence from limited, noisy, and individually variable input. The resulting poverty-of-the-stimulus challenge placed pressure on empiricists to propose more powerful learning mechanisms.

The nativist program then expanded beyond language. The core cognition hypothesis proposes that evolution supplies early conceptual resources for physical objects, number, and minds or agents. Infant studies using looking time and other measures report expectations concerning object permanence, continuous motion, small-number tracking, approximate magnitudes, goals, rational action, cooperation, and beliefs. Such findings make it difficult to regard infants as blank slates, but they do not by themselves establish that an adult concept is fully present at birth. The entry emphasizes distinctions between different systems—for example, approximate number, limited object tracking, and exact numerical competence.

The final part considers alternatives and developments favorable to empiricism. Connectionist and dynamic-systems models reject or revise classical symbol-manipulation accounts, while Bayesian models show how background information can make rapid learning possible. Yet these
key_ideas: Chomsky’s critique of behaviorist language theory shifted attention from observable speech alone to the internal representations and rules that support linguistic competence.

The nativist argument depends partly on the complexity of grammar, the limited and imperfect linguistic input children receive, and the fact that children converge on similar systems without extensive correction.
Developmental research inspired by this debate investigates early competencies in separate domains rather than assuming one uniform, domain-general sequence of stages.

Evidence from infants supports early expectations about object continuity, approximate number, goal-directed action, perspective, and social evaluation, but the interpretation of these results remains contested.

Connectionist, dynamic-systems, and Bayesian approaches restore a larger role for learning. They do not automatically imply empiricism, because their initial structures or prior probabilities may themselves be built in.

The question is not simply whether a capacity is innate. Researchers must ask which representations, processing mechanisms, and learning processes are present initially and how they interact over development.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it concerns what human beings are like before teaching and culture have done much work. It also shapes theories of language, perception, reasoning, development, and social understanding. A good account must explain both the striking abilities of infants and the large gap between infant competence and adult knowledge. The entry suggests that neither “everything is built in” nor “everything is learned from experience” is a sufficiently precise conclusion. Contemporary research instead asks how evolved structures, representations, maturation, learning algorithms, and social input combine. It also shows why philosophical analysis remains important: experimental results

important_terms.definition: A family of views holding that some cognitive structures or representations are part of an organism’s initial biological endowment.
A family of views emphasizing experience, association, and general learning processes as the basis of knowledge.
Chomsky’s framework for describing a language’s rule system, including the sentences it can generate and their sound and meaning.
An argument claiming that the available learning evidence is insufficient to determine the complex rule system acquired, unless learners have additional constraints or information.
A proposed mental architecture containing relatively specialized systems for handling particular kinds of input or tasks.
The hypothesis that evolution provides early conceptual systems for domains such as physical objects, approximate number, and minds or agents.
A probabilistic approach that updates the plausibility of hypotheses using evidence together with prior probabilities.
A model using interconnected simple units whose connection strengths change as the system responds to experience.

questions_to_think_about: Does early sensitivity to an event show that an infant possesses a full concept, or only a more limited expectation?
Can a powerful general learning system explain language acquisition without language-specific innate information?
If a Bayesian model begins with informative priors, are those priors learned, domain-general, or innate?
Why might success on a nonverbal infant task and failure on a verbal preschool task be compatible?
Does evolutionary preparedness support a broad nativist theory of cognition, or only particular domain-specific abilities?

summaries.example: Suppose a baby sees a ball roll behind a screen. When the screen is lifted, the baby looks longer if the ball seems to have vanished or if another object appears where the ball should be. Researchers may infer that the baby expected the ball to continue existing behind the screen. This does not necessarily mean the baby has the same complete idea of an object that an adult has. It may mean that the baby has an early mental rule that objects do not simply disappear.
summaries.summary:
This entry studies the renewed debate between nativism and empiricism about the origins of human knowledge. Nativists argue that some important mental resources are present in the organism’s initial condition. Empiricists emphasize perception, experience, and general learning processes. The dispute is not perfectly simple, because different theories define “innate,” “knowledge,” and “learning” in different ways.

The modern revival of nativism is closely connected with Noam Chomsky’s criticism of behaviorist accounts of language. Chomsky treated grammar as a mental rule system and argued that children master complicated linguistic patterns despite receiving limited, incomplete, and variable examples. This poverty-of-the-stimulus argument made it harder to explain language using only simple associations. It also encouraged researchers to look for early cognitive structures outside language.

Developmental researchers influenced by this approach proposed core cognition: several domain-specific systems that help infants organize experience. Studies suggest that young infants expect hidden objects to persist and move continuously, distinguish approximate quantities, track a small number of individual objects, and interpret some actions as goal-directed. Other experiments suggest early sensitivity to agents’ perspectives, beliefs, cooperation, and intentions. However, these experiments do not settle exactly what babies represent, nor do they show that every adult ability is present from birth. Development involves maturation, learning, language, and social experience.

The entry also discusses empirically friendly approaches. Connectionist models learn through changing patterns of activation, and dynamic-systems models describe development as changing over time. Bayesian**
key_ideas: The nativism-empiricism debate asks whether important knowledge is built into our biological starting point or learned from experience.
Chomsky’s work on language challenged behaviorist explanations by focusing on the complex mental rules children master with limited direct instruction.
Researchers later applied similar questions to babies’ understanding of objects, number, goals, and other minds.
Early abilities do not automatically equal complete adult concepts. For example, babies can track only small sets of objects, while approximate quantity works differently.
Connectionism and Bayesian approaches give learning a larger role, but they can still include built-in starting structures or expectations.
The evidence supports a mixed and carefully divided picture rather than a simple choice between “born knowing everything” and “born knowing nothing”.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it changes how we think about children’s abilities and about learning itself. If children begin with useful mental structures, development is not simply the gradual filling of an empty container. If general learning is more powerful than older empiricists assumed, experience may explain more than early theories allowed. The debate also teaches an important research lesson: evidence for an early ability must be interpreted carefully, because a behavior such as looking longer can reveal an expectation without proving the presence of a complete adult-like concept.

important_terms.definition: The view that some knowledge or mental abilities are part of our starting condition rather than learned wholly from experience.
The view that knowledge develops from experience, often through general learning or association.
A system of rules that describes which sentences belong to a language and how they are connected with sound and meaning.
The challenge that children acquire complex knowledge even though their experience may not contain enough information to determine it by simple learning alone.
The idea that the mind may contain partly specialized systems for different kinds of information.
The proposal that humans begin with several basic conceptual systems, including systems for objects, quantity, and agents.
A way of updating the likelihood of different explanations by combining new evidence with earlier expectations.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between having an early expectation and having a fully developed concept?
Why did Chomsky think that language learning was difficult for a simple experience-based theory to explain?
Could a baby’s longer looking time have more than one possible explanation?
Which parts of mathematical ability might begin with approximate quantity, and which might require language or teaching?
How might built-in abilities and learning from other people work together?
